clue.text: People appear quite small in this race

definitions.text: People appear quite small in this race

parts.words: People appear quite small in this race
parts.note: a painter's term for the band of a view between foreground and background, where figures look small, doubles as the athletics category between sprints and long runs

explanation.surface: A spectator remarks that runners look tiny in a particular event.
explanation.definitionFit: Races of 800 to 1500 metres form this athletics category, and in a picture it is the zone where figures shrink.

clue.text: Use money for improper purposes — mark is suitable

parts.note: M stands for the mark, the former German currency
taken as written
appropriate means suitable or fitting

explanation.surface: A remark that spending funds on bad causes is fine.
explanation.definitionFit: To embezzle or divert funds wrongly, taking them for an unauthorised use.

clue.text: Philosophical theory not providing a single answer

definitions.text: Philosophical theory not providing a single answer

parts.words: Philosophical theory not providing a single answer
parts.note: a doctrine that explains reality by two principles, such as mind and matter, rather than one

explanation.surface: A school of philosophy that refuses to give one neat solution.
explanation.definitionFit: The doctrine that reality has two basic substances, mind and matter, rather than one.

clue.text: Cautious, in general, going over tracks

indicators.note: in a down clue the general's name sits on top of the tracks, going over them

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate general of the American Civil War
RY is short for railway, a set of tracks

explanation.surface: A careful military leader is crossing a railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in general' reads as 'usually'; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Wary and suspicious, unwilling to trust readily.

clue.text: Liable to get broken English with strange dialect

indicators.note: something strange is out of its usual order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone liable to mangle the language, speaking an odd regional tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges DIALECT to DELICAT; 'broken English' looks like a phrase but 'broken' belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fragile, easily damaged or snapped.

clue.text: Hard agreement secured in a way that's extremely cautious

indicators.note: the letters for hard and agreement are fixed inside the abbreviation for a road, a container signal

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
yes is a word of agreement

explanation.surface: A hard-won deal is reached in a very wary manner.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of timid or bashful, meaning most reluctant or wary.

clue.text: Stars in group are involved with odd man out

indicators.note: letters that are involved are tangled together, so the whole pool is rearranged
out means the letters of odd man are knocked out of their order

explanation.surface: Celebrities in a band get mixed up with the misfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' scrambles ODDMAN, and 'involved' mixes those letters with ARE; 'odd man out' looks like the idiom for a misfit.
explanation.definitionFit: A northern constellation, a named group of stars, also holding a nearby galaxy.

clue.text: Insensitive demand by America? Nothing in it

indicators.note: the zero goes inside the whole preceding phrase, so this is a container signal

parts.note: a call for something is a demand
US is the United States of America
O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A heartless demand from the States, with nothing behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard-hearted and unfeeling towards others' suffering.

clue.text: Couple each given half a crown?

definitions.text: Couple each given half a crown?

parts.words: Couple each given half a crown?
parts.note: a husband and wife who shared the English throne as joint monarchs from 1689

explanation.surface: Two people are each handed an old coin worth two shillings and sixpence.
explanation.walkthrough: A half-crown was an old British coin worth two shillings and sixpence; here it is half of a royal crown.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint sovereigns who ruled England, Scotland and Ireland together after 1688.

clue.text: Coach has to gamble on dramatic performance

parts.note: a stagecoach, or stage, was a horse-drawn coach on a set route
to play is to gamble, as at cards or the tables

explanation.surface: A coach driver bets on a show in the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama written for performance in a theatre, as opposed to one for radio or screen.

clue.text: Capital husband put into specialist store

indicators.note: the husband's letter is placed inside the word for the shop, so it is a container signal

parts.note: a deli is a delicatessen, a shop selling fine foods

explanation.surface: A capital-letter husband gets placed into a delicatessen.
explanation.definitionFit: New Delhi is the capital city of India, and the wider city carries this name.

clue.text: Work at taking in old writer

indicators.note: the word for working at something takes the little word in into its middle, so it is a container signal

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it

explanation.surface: Someone works at a job while taking in a classical author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is not a link here: it is the very letters put inside PLY by 'taking'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger were Roman authors of the first century.

clue.text: Twin given bribe to produce lubricant

parts.note: Castor and Pollux are the heavenly twins of Greek myth
to oil someone's palm is to bribe them, so oil is a bribe

explanation.surface: One of a pair of twins is paid off to make a greasing agent.
explanation.definitionFit: This bean-derived oil is used as a lubricant in engines as well as a laxative.

clue.text: Tries to break into English port

definitions.meaning: batters an entrance, as a battering ram would a fortress door
a seaside town and harbour on the Kent coast

explanation.surface: Someone attempts a break-in at a harbour town in England.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the first sense is a ram butting a gate; RAMSGATE is a port in Kent, in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbour town on the Isle of Thanet in Kent, with ferry links to the Continent.

clue.text: Fowl more than a pound — dear in Scotland

parts.note: a guinea was an old British sum of twenty-one shillings, one pound and a shilling
hen is a Scottish term of endearment for a woman, like dear

explanation.surface: A bird costs over a pound, which is expensive north of the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dear' suggests expensive but is a term of affection.
explanation.definitionFit: A speckled African game bird, kept domestically for eggs and meat.

clue.text: Oriental's companion might reveal his age

indicators.note: rearranging the letters of the phrase could uncover something new, so this signals an anagram

explanation.surface: A friend of an Eastern man could give away how old he is.
explanation.definitionFit: A Japanese hostess trained to entertain male guests with conversation, music and dance.

clue.text: Girl — right one to put in top group

indicators.note: the letters for right and one are placed inside the phrase for the top group, a container signal

parts.note: Class A is the highest category or grade
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A girl is told the right person belongs among the leaders.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, as in Richardson's novel heroine.

clue.text: People taken in by Republicans

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the longer word, which takes them in, so this signals a concealed run

explanation.surface: Ordinary voters are fooled by a party's politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: The general populace, the people at large, as in members of the public.

clue.text: As found in odd parts of Bombay, this sort of rice

indicators.note: the two-letter word sits inside the chosen letters, so it is a container signal
the first, third and fifth letters of the following words are picked, the odd ones

explanation.surface: Grains sold in strange districts of an Indian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Odd letters of 'Bombay, this' give BMATI; 'As' goes in after the B. 'this' does double duty only in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-grain fragrant variety grown in India and Pakistan.

clue.text: Confused nobody in the dock?

definitions.meaning: if every ship is out on the ocean, none is moored in port

explanation.surface: An empty prisoner's dock in court leaves everyone baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the dock' suggests a courtroom; here it is where ships berth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for being bewildered pictures a sailor far from land with no bearings.

clue.text: Pessimistic principle derivable from old saws

indicators.note: the answer can be drawn out of the letters by reworking them, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gloomy rule follows from ancient proverbs.
explanation.walkthrough: SOD'S LAW, the British saying that whatever can go wrong will, is fittingly hidden in old sayings.
explanation.definitionFit: The jokey rule that if something can go wrong it will, a gloomy maxim.

clue.text: Wild animals precisely in the middle of vessel

indicators.note: the phrase for exactly goes inside the ship abbreviation, a container signal

parts.note: SS stands for steamship, a vessel
to a T means exactly, precisely

explanation.surface: Beasts are found right in the centre of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Small carnivores of the weasel family, untamed creatures.

clue.text: Revised one script for "Morse", for example

indicators.note: a revised text has been reworked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rewritten screenplay is prepared for the TV detective series.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is the Oxford detective of Colin Dexter's novels and a long-running British TV series.
explanation.definitionFit: Morse holds the police rank of detective inspector, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Paddy's swearing to raise issue

definitions.meaning: an Irish mild oath, Paddy being a crossword name for an Irishman
to become a father, issue meaning offspring

explanation.surface: An Irishman curses as he brings up a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as BE DAD, the second sense is to father children; 'issue' looks like a complaint but means children.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish exclamation, a softened form of 'by God', used as a mild oath.

clue.text: Poet is being passionate

definitions.meaning: Robert ..., the national poet of Scotland
feels fierce desire or anger, glows with feeling

explanation.surface: A writer of verse is feeling intense.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns wrote Scots verse; to feel fervour is to be on fire with emotion.

clue.text: Tutors primarily employed by a head to do this

definitions.text: Tutors primarily employed by a head to do this

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word for tutors is wanted, as in its primary position

parts.note: each means per head, as in five pounds a head

explanation.surface: Tutors are hired by a headmaster to carry out instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employed by' joins the pieces; the whole clue also says what tutors are hired by a head teacher for.
explanation.definitionFit: Instructing pupils is exactly the job tutors are hired by a headmaster to do.

clue.text: A lake in the interior of one country or another

indicators.note: the article and lake letters go inside the first nation's name, so this is a container signal

parts.note: Austria is a European nation, one country among many
L is the usual map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A lake lies in the heart of some nation or other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' is the definition: putting AL inside one country makes a second one.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a second nation, distinct from the first one used in the wordplay.

clue.text: Regular columns giving remarkable view of Northern Ireland

definitions.text: Regular columns giving remarkable view of Northern Ireland

parts.words: Regular columns giving remarkable view of Northern Ireland
parts.note: describes the famous basalt formation on the Antrim coast, tens of thousands of interlocking hexagonal pillars

explanation.surface: A tourist admires orderly pillars in a striking Ulster landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: This Antrim coastal site of hexagonal basalt pillars is a World Heritage scenic wonder.
